body_text:
Cauchy's Integral Formula and Higher Derivatives.

Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be an open domain, let $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$ be holomorphic, and let
$\gamma$ be a positively oriented simple closed contour in $U$ whose interior $\operatorname{Int}(\gamma)$
is contained in $U$. Then for every point $z_0 \in \operatorname{Int}(\gamma)$:
$$ f(z_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz. $$

*Derivation*: By the deformation of contours (Cauchy's theorem on multiply connected domains), the
contour $\gamma$ may be shrunk to an arbitrarily small circle $C_\varepsilon = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - z_0| = \varepsilon\}$
centered at $z_0$. Writing $z = z_0 + \varepsilon e^{i\theta}$ with $dz = i\varepsilon e^{i\theta} d\theta$:
$$ \oint_{C_\varepsilon} \frac{dz}{z - z_0} = \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{i\varepsilon e^{i\theta}}{\varepsilon e^{i\theta}}\,d\theta = 2\pi i. $$
Now decomposing $f(z) = f(z_0) + (f(z) - f(z_0))$:
$$ \oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz = \oint_{C_\varepsilon} \frac{f(z_0)}{z - z_0}\,dz + \oint_{C_\varepsilon} \frac{f(z) - f(z_0)}{z - z_0}\,dz = 2\pi i f(z_0) + \oint_{C_\varepsilon} \frac{f(z) - f(z_0)}{z - z_0}\,dz. $$
By the continuity of $f$ at $z_0$, for any $\delta > 0$ we can choose $\varepsilon$ so small that
$|f(z) - f(z_0)| < \delta$. Applying the $ML$-inequality:
$$ \left| \oint_{C_\varepsilon} \frac{f(z) - f(z_0)}{z - z_0}\,dz \right| \le \frac{\delta}{\varepsilon} (2\pi\varepsilon) = 2\pi\delta \to 0. $$
Taking $\delta \to 0$ proves the formula.

*Higher Derivatives and Cauchy Estimates*: Differentiating under the integral sign $n$ times yields:
$$ f^{(n)}(z_0) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i} \oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz. $$
This demonstrates that every holomorphic function is automatically infinitely differentiable ($C^\infty$).
Furthermore, bounding the integral on a circle of radius $R$ yields *Cauchy's Estimate*:
$$ |f^{(n)}(z_0)| \le \frac{n! M_R}{R^n}, \quad \text{where } M_R = \max_{|z - z_0| = R} |f(z)|. $$

*Liouville's Theorem*: If $f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ is an *entire* function (holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$)
and bounded ($|f(z)| \le M$ for all $z \in \mathbb{C}$), then for $n = 1$:
$$ |f'(z_0)| \le \frac{M}{R} \quad \text{for every } R > 0. $$
Sending $R \to \infty$ forces $f'(z_0) = 0$ for all $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, proving that $f$ is constant.
This immediately proves the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: if a nonconstant polynomial $P(z)$ had no roots,
then $1/P(z)$ would be a bounded entire function, hence constant, contradiction!
